Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Riding for a cause.

Summary:
the story is about a guy called Javier de la Varga – he’s a Spaniard (although he speaks – or writes, at least – good English). He’s spent the past 4 years (1805 days) continuously cycling around the world. I’ve attached a picture of his progress last time I spoke to him. His aim – as well as to cycle the whole world, literally – is to photograph the places he visits and to draw attention to the lives of those living in poverty and hardship. He told me he thinks it will take him a total of 10 years to finish his journey.

He tells us he has lots of footage we can count on using, as well as lots of timelapse footage like in the YouTube clip above. If we want him to record anything specific, we can also let him know.

He arrives in SA in mid-December and will be here until about February, when he plans to travel to South America by boat to begin the next leg of his journey. So we can organise an interview for January. But he says we might be interested in filming his arrival at the Cape of Good Hope – he’ll keep us updated with his estimated date of arrival, but it’ll be while CB offices are closed.

His has given us an excessive on his footage and his story.

Press Release:


Decade on a Bicycle
Spaniard Javier Martinez recently cycled into Cape Town after five-and-a-half years on the seat of a bicycle. His mission for the next four is to complete his decade-long journey around the planet on two wheels. Carte Blanche meets a survivor of war zones, illnesses and more, a man who gave up a promising career as a war photographer to live the simplest life possible and document images of hope the world over.


Script:


67 000 kilometers – that’s how much Spaniard Javier Martinez has clocked up so far in, what he calls, an adventure of a life time – cycling Around the world – often staying in remote villages and destinations off the beaten track.

LINK: Javier has been peddling around the world for the last five and half years. His latest leg has taken him all the way through Africa. We've come here to Langebaan about 110km outside Cape Town to have a conversation with him.

John: Javier good to see you! You well?
Javier: John good to see you!
John: You must be exhausted
Javier: A little bit yah the wind, sunny, sandy, a lot of traffic but you have a beautiful country hey?
John: It is beautiful isn’t it?
Javier: Nice people yah!

Javier, the middle of three children, grew up in Spain and from a young age always had an adventurous spirit.

Javier: I always had a fascination for nature, but travelling it became since I was very very young, like 5 or 6 years, I always has a fascination for maps.

That interest led him to the UK in his early twenties where he trained as a photographer. He then travelled the world as a photojournalist covering conflict areas.

LINK: Javier's life took an unexpected turn when in 2009 he was filming an outbreak of unrest in the Middle East.

He was documenting a demonstration in the Palestinian territories.

Javier: And one of the guys was carrying a kite with the rainbow colors. He was shot five metres away from me by the Israeli soldiers on the other side.

A Palestinian civilian died in front of him.

Javier: That was one of the moments that showed me I am not ready to do war photography. It’s very sad. I can't handle that story. If I do more I lose the humanity I want to keep. So I decided that I wanted to cycle, to travel the world and to show more than bad stories, happy stories.

Javier would carry the bare minimum for his epic journey.

John: Javier this is like an apartment on two wheels. Take us through what you have here.
Javier: Its more that an apartment its more like a house and a life altogether. This is the bedroom where I have the sleeping things. This is the closet, shoes and clothes. This is the office where I have my camera. This one is the bathroom where I have the washing, towels and the medical kit and this one is the kitchen where I have the stove, the pots and a chopping board for vegetable at night. This is the most useful thing, this is the water. I carry like two, which is 4 and half liters. Honey, petrol for cooking, and a good Spanish olive oil.
John: It has to be Spanish?
Javier: Of course.

His adventure started in September 2010 in Indonesia. The Asian leg of his around the world trip. His bike was sponsored but he funded himself from is photojournalism, spending just a few dollars a day on food.

Javier: Indonesia is not jus the most beautiful country in the world, it was my first country cycling so I was new everything was fresh, I was amazed by everything.

Javier spent much of his time taking spectacular shots of Indonesia and the Asian countries that he travelled through. He would tend to stay in the more remote areas to live and breathe each countries unique culture. A highlight for Javier was the winter he spent cycling and hiking in the Himalayas.

Javier: It was amazing you know. I did part of the Himalayas in the winter time when I was camping at -42 degrees but I think always the harder the way, is the nicer the destiny, you get more challenge.

He spent two and half months travelling through Iran before he faced a real test of character when he was caught in a snow blizzard for 4 days in Armenia.

Javier: I went through this pass. I was stuck in the snow storm so I couldn’t go back and ahead of me I had like 20km of deep deep snow which I have no water, no food.

Fortunately he stumbled upon a deserted army truck and found a jar of jam in the cab but the snow kept falling.

Javier: And I thought to myself if it keeps snowing like this tonight I will be dead. I cannot go back I cannot go forwards. Luckily it was very windy, it removed the very thin snow and I was able to push the bike next 4km in 12 hours.
John: That’s extraordinary.
Javier: Its very interesting how my mind went into the, it turned into instinct mechanic. I wasn’t thinking it was just my mind telling me go, go, go.

He arrived in Europe in the summer of 2013 and headed for his hometown in Spain. There he saw his proud dad for the first time in 3 years. All his friends were there to welcome him.

Javier: After Asia, Europe is let’s say, it’s boring. You know I grew up in Europe; Europe is the continent of money. There is no, we lost most of the human values there. Everyone stays in the houses. There is no life on the street; everything closes at 5 o clock.

His African odyssey began in December 2013 when he crossed into Morocco.

Javier: Asia is the continent of diversity, Africa is the continent of warm, and the people are very warm people.

He would spend two years travelling the continent. Witnessing first hand the amazing contrast Africa offers. But he had to be on his toes, Ebola was at its peak in West Africa

LINK: West Africa is very wild, its very wild I was there when there was Ebola so I was stuck at the borders. The corruption is part of the daily life, the cities are quite dangerous, traffic is horrible but the people are amazing and what make travelling is the people, it’s not the other things.

But he had to keep up his guard for unexpected perils.

Link: In Nigeria Javier's Mediterranean appearance became somewhat of a curse. He was often mistaken for a member of the militant group Boko Haram.

Javier: so I got attacked 10 times or more thinking I was a jihadist, I was a suicide bomber. One day I was going to the church to look for shelter and I saw as I went inside the church all the people started running away. Screaming. So the police came and arrested me. They find out, show them the passport, explain what I am doing and they find out I am a normal guy but still you need to go through this in every village in every town.

The highlight of Javier’s epic journey in Africa was his time spent in the Congo basin rain forest where he experienced raw nature, wildlife and untouched landscapes. But on a journey like this there is only so much one can plan for, the rest is left to chance.

Link: For example not being able to cross a border because immigration official has gone on holiday, with the visa stamp.

And that’s what happened when he tried to leave the Congo republic for the DRC. He was stuck for a week. Despite Africa's challenges, Javier spoke of the incredible warmth and hospitality he experienced on the continent. He stayed safe by camping, mostly in rural areas and villages where he soaked up the rich culture and always to the delight of children who were drawn to him like a magnet. Javier shared all his experiences with friends, family and followers on his social media.

John: Even with the technology, I would imagine that being on a bicycle by yourself for long periods of time must be quite lonely. You get to spend a lot of time with yourself,

JAVIER: I feel lonely in the areas where are people. In the areas there is no one, I don’t feel lonely. For example in the Sahara desert, Congo forest, the Namibian desert I’m camping there, I feel the happiest person ever.

When Javier crossed into Namibia in December he had ridden through 33 Africans countries survived two bouts typhoid and malaria in Ghana and Zambia. Cape Town was now within his grasp. In Langabaan he up his tent at the Farmhouse Hotel, one night to go before the final push to Cape Town. After a good meal, we insisted despite his protestations, that he accepts our offer of a room.

Javier: Last night before Cape Town, I’m going to sleep like a proper king. Saving my energy for tomorrow.

6,30 and Javier was off, 110km to go, he had to contend with the sweltering heat and the strong headwind.

Javier: There’s Table Mountain!

He made it in just 7 hours. It was a special moment when he entered the V&A Waterfront. Sorry I'm a bit sweaty John.
And then for the most famous photograph of all, table mountain as a backdrop.

He's been in the saddle for 5 and half years now and a cold South African beer couldn’t have tasted better. Javier plans to publish a book when he has completed his journey to showcase the planets most inspiring and visual stories.

LINK: Alight time for a situation report. We have five damaged spokes on the ear wheel. Plenty of scratches and dents on the frame and very bald front tyre. Much like a car, this bicycle is going to need a major service before Javier embarks on the next leg of this extraordinary journey.

And that will be South and North America with the final leg being Australia and New Zealand. 9-10 years in all.

Tourists and South Africans are fascinated to hear of Javier's adventures and he is making plenty of new friends in Cape Town. He managed to cycle half the world without being robbed but perhaps true to form he was mugged in Cape Town on his 2nd day here. But it hasn’t fazed him. 'He is loving the city and it is time now for him to rest.

Javier: After resting in Cape Town for some time, eating well, meeting people, next one is down down there, the other side of the ocean, South America. All the way from South America to Alaska. Another 3 years cycling more. I hope.

metadata.Summary: the story is about a guy called Javier de la Varga – he’s a Spaniard (although he speaks – or writes, at least – good English). He’s spent the past 4 years (1805 days) continuously cycling around the world. I’ve attached a picture of his progress last time I spoke to him. His aim – as well as to cycle the whole world, literally – is to photograph the places he visits and to draw attention to the lives of those living in poverty and hardship. He told me he thinks it will take him a total of 10 years to finish his journey. He tells us he has lots of footage we can count on using, as well as lots of timelapse footage like in the YouTube clip above. If we want him to record anything specific, we can also let him know. He arrives in SA in mid-December and will be here until about February, when he plans to travel to South America by boat to begin the next leg of his journey. So we can organise an interview for January. But he says we might be interested in filming his arrival at the Cape of Good Hope – he’ll keep us updated with his estimated date of arrival, but it’ll be while CB offices are closed.
